title: IPv6, Multicast, and Anycast: Addressing, Configuration, and Deployment
source_scope: The full IPv6 Markdown guide is preserved. Cross-topic coverage searches are limited to networking lecture guides 01–06; algorithms lectures are excluded.

lessons.title: Why IPv6 exists
learning_goals: Explain IPv4 scarcity and why CIDR/NAT delayed migration.
Distinguish address sharing from a larger hierarchical address space.

lessons.title: Regional allocation and depletion
learning_goals: Identify the RIR allocation hierarchy and depletion milestones.
Interpret consumption models without confusing projections, restrictions, and measurements.

lessons.title: IPv6 notation, compression, and prefixes
learning_goals: Expand and compress IPv6 addresses without changing their value.
Interpret prefix lengths and distinguish valid syntax from canonical form.

lessons.title: Delivery types and global unicast structure
learning_goals: Distinguish unicast, multicast, anycast, and the absence of broadcast.
Read the global-prefix, subnet, and interface-ID fields.

lessons.title: Local scope, special addresses, and embedded IPv4
learning_goals: Explain link-local scope, zone indices, ULAs, and special addresses.
Distinguish mapped, compatible, 6to4, and NAT64 address forms.

lessons.title: Subnetting a site allocation
learning_goals: Calculate the number of /64 LANs in an allocation.
Assign subnet IDs and interpret the five-link worked topology.

lessons.title: Static router and host configuration
learning_goals: Separate interface addressing from forwarding configuration.
Choose a reachable gateway and explain the stability of link-local next hops.

lessons.title: Router advertisements, SLAAC, and DHCPv6
learning_goals: Compare SLAAC, stateless DHCPv6, and stateful DHCPv6.
Distinguish autonomous prefix configuration from router and DNS discovery.

lessons.title: Deriving modified EUI-64 identifiers
learning_goals: Insert ff:fe and invert the U/L bit in a MAC-derived IID.
Check the source examples and distinguish interface-specific assignments.

lessons.title: Stable and temporary interface identifiers
learning_goals: Explain MAC-based tracking and alternative IID lifetimes.
Avoid inferring a configuration mechanism from matching suffixes alone.

lessons.title: ICMPv6 and router discovery
learning_goals: Identify RS, RA, NS, and NA as message types.
Explain solicited versus periodic RAs, source scope, and router lifetime.

lessons.title: Solicited-node multicast and address resolution
learning_goals: Derive a solicited-node group and Ethernet destination from the target address.
Trace NS/NA and distinguish the multicast destination from the unicast target.

lessons.title: Duplicate detection and ICMPv6 filtering
learning_goals: Trace DAD and explain what silence can and cannot establish.
Explain why blocking all ICMPv6 breaks essential control functions.

lessons.title: Multicast replication, membership, and scope
learning_goals: Explain branch replication and multicast forwarding state.
Distinguish MLD/IGMP listener information from multicast routing.

lessons.title: Anycast, DNS selection, and service continuity
learning_goals: Contrast route-selected instances with multicast and DNS-based address selection.
Explain root service replication and stateful-session risks during route changes.

lessons.title: Reading the fixed IPv6 base header
learning_goals: Interpret Flow Label, Payload Length, Next Header, and Hop Limit.
Calculate the 40-byte layout without confusing payload and packet lengths.

lessons.title: Source fragmentation and modular extension headers
learning_goals: Explain why IPv6 routers do not fragment and the source can use an extension.
Trace header chaining and distinguish optional IPsec from automatic protection.

lessons.title: Extension-header deployment and SRv6
learning_goals: Distinguish a standardized extension from usability on a deployed path.
Explain segment steering in a controlled operator domain.

lessons.title: Coexistence, encapsulation, and historical 6to4
learning_goals: Contrast dual stack, tunnelling, and translation.
Trace IPv6 inside IPv4 and derive a historical 6to4 prefix.

lessons.title: NAT64, DNS64, and 464XLAT
learning_goals: Trace IPv4 application traffic through CLAT and PLAT.
Distinguish translation, DNS synthesis, and stateful versus stateless components.

lessons.title: Dual-stack, IPv6-mostly, and IPv6-only access
learning_goals: Compare native access models and their compatibility needs.
Explain IPv6-Only Preferred signalling without assuming every remote service is IPv6.

lessons.title: Interpreting IPv6 adoption measurements
learning_goals: Identify measurement population, method, and observation period.
Separate dated proportions from current traffic volumes and formal uncertainty.

lessons.title: Testing economic explanations for deployment
learning_goals: Compare address prices and device costs without conflating denominators.
Assess proposed adoption drivers without inferring causality from correlation.

lessons.title: Happy Eyeballs and hidden path failures
learning_goals: Explain how successful fallback can hide a broken address family.
Distinguish per-family monitoring from aggregate reachability and lost translation state.

lessons.title: Worked checks and practical revision
learning_goals: Connect notation, subnetting, IIDs, ND, and header calculations.
Inspect configurations while distinguishing observations from assumptions.

question_links.rationale: NAT address sharing and address/transport rewriting are described, and routing teaches the end-to-end principle. The guides do not explain the claimed obstruction of protocol innovation or make the keyed tradeoff a complete answer to exhaustion.
question_links.next_action: Review missing teaching and any wording issue; do not assign a lesson or fill a gap silently.
question_links.review_note: The stem asks why NAT cannot fully solve address exhaustion, but the key gives transparency/innovation costs rather than the finite-space limit. That protocol-innovation claim also needs teaching not supplied by these guides.

question_links.rationale: The configuration-method comparison teaches SLAAC and its actual dependencies. The wording review explains why that mechanism alone does not answer the stated end-to-end-connectivity claim.
question_links.next_action: Review the wording before scored practice; the original key is unchanged.
question_links.review_note: SLAAC automates address formation; it does not establish end-to-end reachability or remove NAT by itself. None of the options clearly names the intended global-addressing benefit. Review the stem/key relationship.

question_links.rationale: The global-unicast layout separates provider routing prefix, site subnet ID, and interface ID, explaining hierarchical delegation.
question_links.next_action: Use the primary lesson plus any additional required lessons; optional links are background.

question_links.rationale: The notation lesson restricts :: to one zero run and preserves nonzero values; it also distinguishes valid syntax from canonical notation. Additional required lesson 05 provides the mixed IPv4/IPv6 notation example needed to assess that option rather than reject all mixed spellings.
question_links.next_action: Review the wording before scored practice; the original key is unchanged.
question_links.review_note: The stem does not distinguish invalid syntax from changing the intended address: repeated :: is invalid syntax, while omitting a nonzero group is not a faithful compression even if the result parses.

question_links.rationale: The anycast lesson explicitly contrasts reaching one route-selected member with multicast delivery to the group.
question_links.next_action: Use the primary lesson plus any additional required lessons; optional links are background.

question_links.rationale: The SLAAC method forms an address from an advertised prefix and local IID without a DHCP address server. MAC derivation is optional, as the wording review notes.
question_links.next_action: Review the wording before scored practice; the original key is unchanged.
question_links.review_note: MAC-based modified EUI-64 is one IID method, not a requirement of SLAAC. The key should identify SLAAC without implying that all SLAAC addresses derive from a MAC.

question_links.rationale: The coexistence lesson explains why IPv6 cannot simply cross a native IPv4-only segment and illustrates the transition mechanism that makes it possible.
question_links.next_action: Use the primary lesson plus any additional required lessons; optional links are background.

question_links.rationale: The tunnel lesson nests an intact IPv6 packet inside IPv4 for transit, then removes the outer header at the far endpoint.
question_links.next_action: Use the primary lesson plus any additional required lessons; optional links are background.

question_links.rationale: The extension-header explanation connects a fixed simple base layout with linked optional functions.
question_links.next_action: Use the primary lesson plus any additional required lessons; optional links are background.

question_links.rationale: The guide teaches source fragmentation and ICMPv6 feedback, but not the 1280-byte minimum link MTU or lower-layer adaptation for smaller frames.
question_links.next_action: Review missing teaching and any wording issue; do not assign a lesson or fill a gap silently.
question_links.review_note: The 1280-byte rule is a minimum IPv6 link-MTU capability, not a minimum packet length. Smaller lower-layer frames require adaptation below IPv6; the keyed phrase conflates these ideas.

question_links.rationale: The source-fragmentation lesson removes inline fragmentation fields and work from forwarding routers, while permitting a source Fragment header.
question_links.next_action: Use the primary lesson plus any additional required lessons; optional links are background.

question_links.rationale: Routing lesson 03 explains why all fragments are needed for reassembly and that IP does not recover a missing fragment. Required IPv6 lesson 17 establishes the IPv6 source-only fragmentation model. The stem asks a qualitative risk, not a numerical loss calculation.
question_links.next_action: Use the primary lesson plus any additional required lessons; optional links are background.

evidence.section: 2. Principles of Reliable Data Transfer and Pipelining

question_links.rationale: Routing teaches best-effort IP and endpoint recovery; TCP explains reliable transport and ACKs. Neither explains the scope and limitations of hop-by-hop link ACKs sufficiently for this comparison.

question_links.rationale: Anycast operation and ordinary route selection are taught, but not the route-scaling tradeoff asked here. The keyed /32 requirement additionally needs correction rather than extra teaching of that false rule.
question_links.next_action: Review missing teaching and any wording issue; do not assign a lesson or fill a gap silently.
question_links.review_note: Anycast does not universally require multiple /32 routes per service. IPv6 host routes use /128; route-scale costs depend on allocation, aggregation, and deployment. The key conflates these matters.

evidence.section: 2.4 Motivating Case Study 1: Inter-Domain Routing (BGP Limitations)

question_links.rationale: DNS teaches replica/query-load distribution and SDN discusses upstream attack filtering, but neither explains anycast distribution of DDoS traffic or its capacity limits.
question_links.next_action: Review missing teaching and any wording issue; do not assign a lesson or fill a gap silently.

question_links.rationale: The anycast service examples explain location-dependent routing to a replica. The wording review preserves the distinction between route preference and geographical proximity.
question_links.next_action: Review the wording before scored practice; the original key is unchanged.
question_links.review_note: Nearest means preferred by routing policy and metrics, not necessarily the geographically closest regional server. The keyed option needs that qualification.

question_links.rationale: Address scalability and header/security mechanisms have support, but the compound keyed summary includes mobility support not taught in the networking guides. Mobile carrier translation is not an explanation of IP mobility.
question_links.next_action: Review missing teaching and any wording issue; do not assign a lesson or fill a gap silently.
question_links.review_note: The key bundles scalability, mobility, security, and QoS. The guide does not teach mobility support; it also explicitly rejects automatic IPv6 security. Header mechanisms are not universal service guarantees.

question_links.rationale: The motivation lesson teaches NAT delaying migration; required lesson 19 supplies IPv4/IPv6 compatibility and transition mechanisms. The explanation supports the qualitative tradeoff, not a measured ranking of all adoption causes.

question_identity: Source indices are zero-based in source_quiz. Verify question_sha256 before matching after edits. Questions remain canonical in their source topic even when another topic provides the primary lesson.
dependency_convention: Mapped questions explicitly distinguish additional required_lesson_ids from optional_lesson_ids; their union is related_lesson_ids. Coverage-gap entries leave dependencies unresolved rather than asserting that no additional teaching is needed.
